Adopt a smooth single-component material continuum on a stated macroscopic regime in a Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ be positive. On each swept material region, require $\rho,u,e,T,s,q,\sigma\in C^1$ and $b,r\in C^0$, with $\rho>0$ and $T>0$; the motion has the regularity and positive Jacobian in the preceding definition. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. The Jordan integral convention for such regions and their smooth images is the one in the mathematical interface identified below. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

The entropy flux uses the local material temperature at the heat-transfer point. A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

Work in the nonrelativistic SI fluid model on an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in seconds and oriented Euclidean three-space measured in metres. Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. A moving solid boundary is locally parameterized by a $C^2$ embedding $X_b:I\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^3$, where $\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open and $D_\xi X_b$ has rank two; its material boundary velocity is $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. The boundary patches have continuous outward Euclidean unit normal $n$. In the smooth branch, assume $u,T,q$ have continuous traces wherever boundary values are imposed. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

At each thermal boundary patch, select and state compatible data of one of these forms: insulation, $q\cdot n=0$; prescribed temperature, $T=T_b$ for a specified field $T_b>0$ in kelvins; or prescribed outward conductive heat flux, $q\cdot n=q_b$ for a specified field $q_b$ in watts per square metre. These are alternative boundary models. Their energy and entropy fluxes are accounted for through the chosen boundary data; no separate surface storage or reservoir entropy law is implicit.

A periodic cell with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z)$. Periodicity identifies opposite faces by the corresponding translations and requires equality of the fields and of each derivative trace required by the selected evolution problem. Paired fluxes then cancel in cell integrals. These identified faces are not physical walls.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, prescribe only the fields present in the selected model. Require them to satisfy the exact function-space regularity, positivity, differential constraints, constitutive state-domain restrictions, and wall or periodic compatibility hypotheses of the particular evolution result being used. In the weak formulation, initial data enter through the test-function initial term; that fixes a distributional initial datum but does not by itself supply a strong trace. This postulate selects model data only. It asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity improvement, approximation, or solvability for any initial-boundary value problem.

Use a Cartesian inertial frame in Newtonian spacetime. At an event let $u$ be the fluid velocity, $T>0$ its temperature, $\rho>0$ its mass density, and $\xi=(\rho,T)$ its local state in a specified open set $\mathcal S\subset(0,\infty)^2$. The velocity gradient has components $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$; define the symmetric rate matrix $D=(L+L^T)/2$, its trace $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D$, and its trace-free part $D_0=D-\theta I_3/3$, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. For $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, use the Frobenius contraction $A:B=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

Adopt specified scalar state laws $\mu,\zeta:\mathcal S\to[0,\infty)$ and a specified conductivity matrix law $K:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, with
$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K=(K+K^T)/2. $$
Assume the viscous response at a fixed state is linear in $D$ and equivariant under proper rotations, and adopt
$$ \tau=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$
Here $p$ is the scalar pressure field in the tension-positive convention: the traction on an outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Under a rigid observer rotation $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$, the tensor fields transform by $S^*=QSQ^T$; $\mu,\zeta$ are scalar state functions and $K^*=QKQ^T$. The closure is therefore form-invariant under those rotations. The mathematical linear-isotropic classification identifies this stress form from the stated linearity and equivariance hypotheses; it does not establish that any material adopts them.

In SI units, $D,\theta,D_0$ are in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\mu,\zeta$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $K$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and $\sigma,\tau,p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. If the same stress is written $2\mu D+\lambda\theta I_3$, then $\lambda=\zeta-2\mu/3$; no nonnegativity of $\lambda$ is assumed. These specified constitutive functions are adopted model inputs, not measured coefficient values or consequences of balance laws.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval and $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ open. A smooth constant-density incompressible Newtonian branch has a constant $\rho_0>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, a constant dynamic shear viscosity $\mu\ge0$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, a velocity field $u\in C^2(\Omega,\mathbb R^3)$, and a pressure multiplier $p\in C^1(\Omega,\mathbb R)$. Define $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D=(L+L^T)/2$, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$. The branch is specified by
$$ \rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma, $$
where $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$. Equivalently, for constant $\mu$, its momentum equation is
$$ \rho_0D_tu+\nabla p=\mu\Delta u,\qquad \Delta u_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_jx_j}u_i. $$
Indeed, $\operatorname{div}(2\mu D)=\mu\Delta u+\mu\nabla(\operatorname{div}u)=\mu\Delta u$. This is the incompressible specialization of the adopted Newtonian closure: $\theta=\operatorname{div}u=0$ implies $D_0=D$, so the bulk-viscosity and Fourier-flux terms do not enter this mechanical equation. The pressure is a constraint multiplier and is not identified with a compressible equation-of-state pressure. Define the kinematic viscosity $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$. Boundary and initial data are not part of this definition, and the item asserts no solution existence.

Let $h,a,\rho_0,\mu>0$, let $p_0,G,V_0,V_1\in\mathbb R$, and set $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. In the constant-density model

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,$$

take the infinite plane channel $\Omega_{\rm ch}=\{(x,y,z):x\in\mathbb R,\ 0<y<h,\ z\in\mathbb R\}$, with $u=(v(y),0,0)$, $p=p_0-Gx$, $v\in C^2([0,h])$, and wall values $v(0)=V_0$, $v(h)=V_1$. Then the unique profile within this ansatz is

$$v(y)=V_0+(V_1-V_0)\frac yh+\frac{G}{2\mu}y(h-y).$$

Its volume flux per unit width in the $z$ direction and its fixed-coordinate shear component are

$$Q_{\rm ch}=\int_0^h v(y)\,dy=\frac h2(V_0+V_1)+\frac{Gh^3}{12\mu},\qquad \sigma_{xy}(0)=\mu\frac{V_1-V_0}{h}+\frac{Gh}{2},\qquad \sigma_{xy}(h)=\mu\frac{V_1-V_0}{h}-\frac{Gh}{2}.$$

For the infinite circular pipe $\Omega_a=\{(x,y,z):x\in\mathbb R,\ y^2+z^2<a^2\}$, take $x$ as the axial coordinate, $r=(y^2+z^2)^{1/2}$, $u=(w(r),0,0)$, $p=p_0-Gx$, and require the radial field $(y,z)\mapsto w((y^2+z^2)^{1/2})$ to be $C^2$ on the closed cross-sectional disk with no slip $w(a)=0$. Then the unique profile within this ansatz is

$$w(r)=\frac{G}{4\mu}(a^2-r^2),\qquad Q_{\rm pipe}=\int_0^a2\pi r\,w(r)\,dr=\frac{\pi G a^4}{8\mu}.$$

Both fields satisfy the exact stationary Navier–Stokes equations for every choice of the positive constants and also satisfy the corresponding steady Stokes equations, because their time derivative and convective acceleration vanish. The pipe uniqueness claim uses regularity on the full disk, including the axis. Both uniqueness claims are restricted to the stated one-dimensional ansatz; neither asserts uniqueness among all flows. The domains are infinite or fully developed and give no finite entrance or exit error estimate. Under SI interpretation, $h,a,x,y,z,r$ are in metres, $u,V_0,V_1,v,w$ in metres per second, $\rho_0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, $\mu$ in pascal-seconds, $\nu$ in square metres per second, $p,p_0$ in pascals, and $G$ in pascals per metre. The channel flux per unit width is in square metres per second and the pipe volume flux is in cubic metres per second.

derivations.claim: In both fields velocity has only an axial component independent of the axial coordinate; hence $\operatorname{div}u=0$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=0$. The plane momentum equation reduces to $\mu v''=-G$, and the pipe equation to $\mu(w''+r^{-1}w')=-G$ for $r>0$. [given, A1, A2, A3, F1, algebra]

Integrating the plane equation twice gives $v(y)=-Gy^2/(2\mu)+C_1y+C_0$. The wall values determine $C_0=V_0$ and $C_1=(V_1-V_0)/h+Gh/(2\mu)$, yielding the stated profile uniquely. Its integral gives $Q_{\rm ch}$; differentiation and $\sigma_{xy}=\mu v'$ give both wall shear values. [given, A2, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

Multiplication of the pipe equation by $r$ gives $(rw')'=-Gr/\mu$. Integration yields $w=-Gr^2/(4\mu)+C\log r+D$ on $r>0$. Full-disk $C^2$ regularity forces $C=0$, and $w(a)=0$ fixes $D=Ga^2/(4\mu)$, proving uniqueness within this ansatz. Integration with area element $2\pi r\,dr$ gives $Q_{\rm pipe}$; differentiation gives $\sigma_{rx}=-Gr/2$. [given, A2, A3, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

Time derivatives and convective accelerations vanish, so each field solves the stationary Navier–Stokes and corresponding steady Stokes equations for every allowed parameter choice, without a limiting or small-parameter hypothesis. This says nothing about finite-device behavior or empirical validity. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval measured in seconds, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ nonempty and open in metres, and $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Use SI units: $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\rho$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $P$ in pascals, and $V,h,B$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$. Let $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ have continuous first time and spatial derivatives, $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time, first spatial and second spatial derivatives, and $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be a time-independent $C^2$ potential per unit mass. Adopt the barotropic Euler equations with conservative body acceleration $-\nabla V$:
$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$
For a fixed $\rho_{\rm ref}>0$, define $h(q)=\int_{\rho_{\rm ref}}^qP'(r)/r\,dr$. A steady streamline is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ satisfying $x'(s)=u(x(s))$. If $u,\rho$ are steady, then
$$B=\frac{|u|^2}{2}+h(\rho)+V$$
is constant along each streamline. If additionally $\operatorname{curl}u=0$ on a connected component, then $B$ is constant throughout that component; here $\operatorname{curl}$ is the Cartesian curl. For every closed $C^1$ material loop $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$, $X_t=u(t,X)$, and continuous $X_s,X_{ts}$, the circulation
$$\Gamma(t)=\int_0^1u(t,X(t,s))\cdot X_s(t,s)\,ds$$
is constant. The conservative body acceleration and local barotropic branch are model inputs; no statement concerns shocks, nonbarotropic pressure, nonconservative forcing, or viscous circulation.

In particular, take $P(\rho)=c^2\rho$ with $c>0$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $V=0$, angular speed $\Omega_0\ne0$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, density $\rho_c,\rho_{\rm ref}>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, angular and reference lengths $R,H$ in metres, and the open cylinder $D=\{(x,y,z):x^2+y^2<R^2,\ |z|<H\}$ for $R,H>0$ measured in metres.
